title: Area VI review: Navigation
intro: These questions mix all four Tasks of Area VI: pilotage and dead reckoning, navigation systems and radar services, diversion and lost procedures. Many join two Tasks in one cross-country, the way a navigation leg on the checkride turns into a diversion or a lost-position problem.

questions.q: Lowering clouds make you divert. You measure a true course of 140 to the alternate. TAS is 120 knots, the wind is from 200 at 30 knots (true) and variation is 8 W. Using the crosswind x 60 / TAS shortcut from the lessons (a pilot technique, not an FAA formula), what magnetic heading do you turn to?
questions.why: The wind is 60 degrees right of the course, so the crosswind is 30 x sin 60 = 26.0 knots and the WCA is about 26.0 x 60 / 120 = 13 degrees. The shortcut is not FAA guidance; it is the small-angle form of the wind triangle and matches the PHAK's own triangle example [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]]. A wind from the right is added: 140 + 13 = 153 true. West variation is added: 153 + 8 = 161 magnetic [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]]. 145 subtracts the west variation. 163 uses the whole 30 knots as crosswind (15 degrees), which overcorrects because the wind is not straight across.

questions.q: Day VFR, an 84 NM leg straight into a forecast 22-knot headwind. TAS is 130 knots and you burn 9.6 GPH at normal cruise. Ignoring taxi and climb, what is the least fuel 14 CFR 91.151 lets you begin the flight with?
options: About 12.3 gallons
About 11.0 gallons
About 14.7 gallons
About 7.5 gallons
questions.why: Fuel follows time, and time follows groundspeed, so use GS when there is wind [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. GS = 130 - 22 = 108 knots; 84 / 108 = 0.778 hr; 0.778 x 9.6 = 7.5 gallons. By day you also need 30 more minutes at normal cruise, 0.5 x 9.6 = 4.8 gallons [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]]. 7.5 + 4.8 = 12.3. 11.0 figures the leg with TAS (84 / 130 x 9.6 = 6.2) and ignores the wind the rule says to consider. 14.7 uses the 45-minute night reserve.

questions.q: Tracking a VOR radial outbound on a commercial checkride leg, you find you are 3 degrees off the radial 36 NM from the station. About how far off course are you, and are you inside the CA.VI.A position standard?
options: About 3 NM; outside the commercial 2 NM standard
About 0.6 NM; well inside the standard
About 1.8 NM; outside, because the commercial standard is 1 NM
About 1.8 NM; inside the commercial 2 NM standard
questions.why: Each degree is 1 NM wide at 60 NM from the station, and the width changes in proportion to distance [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]]. At 36 NM one degree is 36 / 60 = 0.6 NM, so 3 degrees is 1.8 NM. The commercial ACS allows 2 NM from the planned route (ACS CA.VI.A.S5), so you pass, with little margin. 3 NM treats every degree as 1 NM wide, which is true only at 60 NM. 0.6 NM is the width of one degree, not three. The private standard is 3 NM (ACS PA.VI.A.S5); no standard is 1 NM.

questions.q: Lost, you tune two identified VORs. On VOR A the needle centers with 045 and FROM. On VOR B it centers with 300 and TO. How do you plot your position on the sectional?
options: Draw 225 outbound from A and 300 outbound from B on each compass rose
Draw 045 outbound from A and 120 outbound from B
Draw 045 outbound from A and 300 outbound from B
Draw 225 outbound from A and 120 outbound from B on each compass rose
questions.why: A centered needle with FROM shows the radial you are on, and with TO it shows the course to the station, the reciprocal of your radial [[1:411|PHAK 16-24]]. So you are on A's 045 radial and B's 120 radial (300 - 180). Draw both outward from the stations' compass roses; where the lines cross is your fix [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Drawing 300 from B puts you on the wrong side of that station.

questions.q: The examiner has failed your heading indicator. You are steady on a west heading by the magnetic compass, then add power and accelerate after a descent. What does the compass do, and what should you do?
options: Nothing; acceleration error happens only on north and south headings, never on east or west
It shows a turn toward south; roll gently right to bring the card back to west, then hold that bank
It shows a real turn toward north, so roll left until it reads west again, then level the wings
It shows a turn toward north; keep the wings level and read it again once speed is steady
questions.why: On east or west headings, accelerating makes the compass show a turn toward north and decelerating shows a turn toward south (ANDS) [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]. The airplane has not turned, so chasing the card with bank puts a real heading error in. Read the compass only in steady, unaccelerated flight, and you still owe the examiner 10 degrees (ACS CA.VI.A.S7). The last option has it backward: holding north or south, a speed change causes no error [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

questions.q: Diverting, your FIS-B NEXRAD image is stamped 2 minutes old. It shows a 12-mile gap between two cells that ATC calls severe. The gap leads straight to your alternate. What do you do?
options: Fly the gap; a 2-minute-old image is current enough
Plan a route or alternate that avoids the whole area
Fly the gap but ask ATC for vectors through it
Fly the gap below the cloud bases, where the air is smoother
questions.why: Data link weather shows where the weather was, and it may be 15 to 20 minutes older than the display says, so it is for avoiding storms entirely, not picking a path through them [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27]]. Avoid any severe thunderstorm by at least 20 miles [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27]], and a 12-mile gap cannot give 20 miles from both cells. Flying under a thunderstorm is a listed don't, even when you can see through [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27]].

questions.q: Before a flight you tune the departure airport's VOT and center the needle. Which reading shows the receiver is inside the 14 CFR 91.171 limit for a VOT check?
options: 184 with FROM
006 with FROM
182 with TO
175 with TO
questions.why: On a VOT, a centered needle should read 0 with FROM or 180 with TO [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]. The VOT limit is plus or minus 4 degrees [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171]]. 182 TO is 2 degrees off, so it passes. 006 FROM and 175 TO are 6 and 5 degrees off. 184 is close to 180, but with FROM showing the reading should be near 0, so it is 176 degrees off, not 4.

questions.q: You become unsure of your position. ATC says it may take 20 minutes to find you, and you will circle a large lake you can identify. Which power setting does the PHAK point to while you wait?
options: The maximum range setting
Full power, to climb as high as possible first
Normal 75 percent cruise, to keep the engine warm
The maximum endurance setting
questions.why: Maximum endurance, the most time in the air for the fuel, is found at the point of minimum power required, where fuel flow is lowest [[1:266|PHAK 11-10]]. Maximum range, at L/D max, is for covering distance, such as heading to a known airport [[1:266|PHAK 11-10]] [[1:265|PHAK 11-9]]. While you circle and wait, time is what matters. Your POH gives the real numbers.

questions.q: You tune a VORTAC for a cross-check. The CDI shows a flag, and you hear only one identifier about every 30 seconds. What does that tell you?
options: The station is in test, so the DME reading is also unusable
The VOR is working, but the DME is off the air
Both are working; the VOR identifier always sounds that slowly
The DME is probably working, but the VOR may not be
questions.why: The DME identifier is sent once for every three or four VOR identifiers. If only one identifier is heard about every 30 seconds, the DME is operative [[33:73|AIM 1-1-7]] and the VOR part is not sending its own identifier. A removed identifier warns that the facility may be unreliable, so do not use it [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]], and the flag agrees. Option 4 needs the T-E-S-T code, which you did not hear.

questions.q: Your magnetic course is 172 over ground near 1,000 ft MSL. The MEF in every quadrant along the route is 4,3, and the tallest charted antenna is 3,980 ft MSL. You decide to use the MEF as your own terrain margin. What is the lowest VFR cruising altitude that fits the course and stays above the MEF?
questions.why: Above 3,000 ft AGL on a magnetic course of 0 to 179 you fly odd thousands plus 500 [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]]. The MEF is a chart figure, not a regulation: 4,3 means 4,300 ft, the highest terrain or obstacle in the quadrant rounded up [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p.12]], and staying above it is the margin you chose. 3,500 is below it. 4,500 would be 520 ft above the antenna, clear of the PHAK's 500 ft floor near antennas [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]], but it is an even altitude, which belongs to courses of 180 to 359 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]]. 6,500 is even too. 5,500 is the lowest that meets both.

questions.q: Your diversion airport is new to you. Your POH landing distance over a 50 ft obstacle is 1,900 ft. The sectional data block shows 26, but the Chart Supplement lists the usable runway as 2,350 ft. Using the RMH personal minimums adjustment, is this runway acceptable?
options: No; the Chart Supplement's 2,350 ft is less than 1,900 + 500 = 2,400 ft
Yes; 2,350 ft is more than the 1,900 ft you need, so no extra margin is required
Yes; the sectional data block shows 2,600 ft, which is more than 1,900 + 500 = 2,400 ft
No; an unfamiliar airport needs double the landing distance, so you need 3,800 ft
questions.why: Use the Chart Supplement over the chart where they differ [[1:404|PHAK 16-17]], and remember the usable length may be less than the charted one [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p.15]]. 14 CFR 91.103(b) requires you to know the runway lengths and your landing distance [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]. For an unfamiliar airport the RMH suggests adding at least 500 ft to required runway length [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]: 1,900 + 500 = 2,400 ft, more than 2,350. Option 2 is legal but skips the margin, and nothing in the sources asks for double.

questions.q: You get lost on a VFR flight plan. After ATC finds you, your new arrival time is 35 minutes later than your filed ETA. What does the AIM say to do?
options: Nothing; FSS waits an hour past the ETA before searching
Report a new ETA to the nearest FSS
Close the flight plan in the air and file a new one
Tell approach, which updates the flight plan for you
questions.why: If your ETE changes by 30 minutes or more, report a new ETA to the nearest FSS. If you fail to respond within one-half hour after your ETA, a search starts [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]. So a 35-minute delay would start an unneeded search. Do not assume ATC passes it on; towers do not close VFR plans for you either [[33:339|AIM 5-1-14]].

questions.q: After a precautionary landing in a remote field, your rental's ELT is an older 121.5 MHz unit. Who can detect its signal?
options: The Cospas-Sarsat satellites, which still monitor 121.5 MHz and alert rescue within minutes
Any Flight Service Station in the region, which can direction-find the signal
Only a nearby ATC facility or an overflying aircraft monitoring 121.5
No one; 121.5 MHz ELTs no longer transmit since the satellites stopped listening
questions.why: Since 2009 Cospas-Sarsat no longer monitors 121.5 MHz or 243.0 MHz. An aircraft with only such an ELT depends on a nearby ATC facility or an overflying aircraft hearing the alert and telling ATC [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]. The ELT still transmits; it just has no satellite listening. Stay with the airplane unless you have good reason to think you will not be found [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]].

questions.q: You are on VFR flight following when you divert to a nontowered field 15 NM away. You want its CTAF to hear the traffic. What should you do?
options: Switch at once; radar service ends automatically when you leave the frequency, so no call is needed
Squawk 1200 first, then change to the CTAF and tell the controller there that you are leaving
Tell the controller you are leaving, change frequency, then squawk 1200 if applicable
Stay on approach until you land, since leaving the frequency would start a search for you
questions.why: When you no longer want advisories, advise the controller before changing frequencies, then squawk 1200 if applicable [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15]]. Service ends automatically only when an arriving VFR aircraft is told by ATC to change to the advisory frequency [[33:218|AIM 4-1-18]]. If radar and radio contact are both lost without a service termination, the facility treats it as a possible emergency [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]], which is why you speak up first rather than stay on the wrong frequency.

questions.q: After a diversion and a 15-minute hold you will land with about 20 minutes of fuel, and you cannot accept any more delay. Approach tells you to expect another 15 minutes of holding. What do you say?
options: Declare an emergency due to low fuel and give fuel remaining in minutes
"Minimum fuel", which tells ATC you need priority handling and puts you at the front
Give fuel remaining in gallons and pounds so ATC can work out your endurance time
Nothing yet; 20 minutes of fuel is still within the 30-minute day reserve, so no call is needed
questions.why: Minimum fuel is only an advisory and does not imply a need for priority. If your fuel suggests you need priority for a safe landing, declare an emergency due to low fuel and report fuel remaining in minutes [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]]. Doubt about fuel endurance already puts you in at least an urgency condition [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. The 30-minute reserve in 14 CFR 91.151 is fuel to begin a flight with, not a point at which you may wait [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]].

questions.q: Your airspeed indicator shows 120 knots (CAS) at 8,000 ft, with no wind. The next checkpoint is 23 NM ahead. Using the PHAK rule of thumb for TAS, about how long until you reach it?
options: About 11.5 minutes
About 10 minutes
About 8.5 minutes
About 12 minutes
questions.why: The rule of thumb adds 2 percent to CAS for each 1,000 ft: 8 x 2 = 16 percent, and 120 x 1.16 = 139 knots TAS [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. With no wind GS equals TAS, and time = distance / GS: 23 / 139 x 60 = 9.9 minutes, about 10 [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. 11.5 minutes uses the indicated 120 knots, which is the speed the airspeed indicator shows, not the speed you move through the air at altitude.

questions.q: Your magnetic course is 214 over ground near 1,000 ft MSL. Haze tops are at 5,800 ft MSL with clear air above, and the clouds are far higher. What is the lowest altitude that fits 14 CFR 91.159 and the AC 90-48E advice about haze?
questions.why: On a magnetic course of 180 to 359 above 3,000 ft AGL you fly even thousands plus 500 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]]. Haze makes other aircraft hard to see, so AC 90-48E recommends flying above a haze layer [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9]]. 6,500 is the lowest even-plus-500 altitude above the 5,800 ft tops. 4,500 fits the course but keeps you in the haze. 5,500 and 7,500 are odd altitudes, which belong to courses of 0 to 179 [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]].

questions.q: You divert to an airport you find by its on-field VOR, in good VFR in the middle of the day. When, by the AFH, is your midair collision risk highest?
options: Within about 5 miles of that airport and near the VOR
At night, when traffic is harder to see
Above the clouds, where nobody expects other aircraft
En route, at the VFR cruising altitude for your course
questions.why: Most midair collisions and near midairs happen in good VFR, in daylight, within 5 miles of an airport and/or near navigation aids [[24:31|AFH 1-10]]. A diversion to a VOR airport puts you there while your eyes are busy. See and avoid is your duty whenever weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]], and the PHAK asks for the same see-and-avoid effort near VORs and NDBs as near VFR waypoints [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Night and above the clouds are not where the AFH puts the risk.

questions.q: Lost late in the day, you check the almanac: sunset is 1812 and evening civil twilight ends at 1840 local. When does night begin under 14 CFR 1.1?
questions.why: Night is the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, converted to local time [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]. So night begins at 1840, not at sunset. Fading light also takes away the landmarks you are using to find yourself, which is why fuel and daylight set the deadline for asking for help.

questions.q: You divert to a field with a VORTAC on it and track inbound at 3,000 ft AGL over hilly ground. The needle starts to swing as you get close. What confirms station passage?
options: The DME reaching 0.0 NM
The needle swinging, since that happens only over the station
The station's Morse identifier fading out
The TO/FROM indicator changing from TO to FROM
questions.why: At some stations, mostly in hilly or mountain areas, a brief needle swing looks like approaching the station, so the AIM says to use the to/from indicator to find positive station passage [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]]. DME shows slant range: 6,076 ft AGL over the station reads about 1.0 NM [[1:414|PHAK 16-27]] [[1:415|PHAK 16-28]], so at 3,000 ft it reads about 3,000 / 6,076 = 0.5 NM, never 0.0. Nothing in the sources ties the identifier to passage.

questions.q: You file a VFR flight plan for a charter using the company call sign, but the ADS-B FLT ID in your airplane is set to the tail number. You ask for flight following. What can happen?
options: Nothing; ATC identifies you by your Mode C altitude and transponder code, so the ID is unneeded
Your TIS-B traffic display turns off until the flight ID and the filed call sign are the same
Your ADS-B Out stops transmitting until the IDs match, so ATC loses your position entirely
ATC may not link you to your flight plan, so services may be delayed or unavailable
questions.why: ATC automation uses the ADS-B FLT ID to identify each aircraft and match it to its filed flight plan. If the two are not identical, a call sign mismatch is generated, ATC may not associate you with your flight plan, and services may be delayed or unavailable until it is fixed [[33:303|AIM 4-5-7]]. ADS-B Out keeps transmitting; if you have it, it must transmit at all times unless ATC says otherwise [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225]].

questions.q: Unsure of your position near a Class C area, you find your tablet's database expired two cycles ago and you cannot update it in flight. How does the PHAK say to treat its moving map?
options: Use it normally for the airspace picture, since 14 CFR has no database currency rule for VFR pilots
Trust it as long as the unit has RAIM and shows a good GPS position on the moving map
Disregard its airspace picture for critical navigation decisions and use the current chart
Use only its named waypoints, which do not change, and ignore the airspace boundaries
questions.why: If an expired database cannot be updated, the PHAK says to disregard any moving map display of airspace for critical navigation decisions, because named waypoints may no longer exist or may have moved, and VFR pilots should rely on current charts [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]]. RAIM watches the satellite signals, not the age of the data [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]]. The first option starts from a true fact but ignores the PHAK: no rule requiring a current database does not make old airspace data right.

questions.q: Diverting, you find a V-airway labeled 230 at a VOR. You are on that airway southwest of the VOR, and the alternate is on the field at the VOR. What rough magnetic course takes you to the alternate?
questions.why: A radial or printed airway is outbound from the station, so to fly to the station you may need the reciprocal [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. You are on the 230 radial, southwest of the VOR, so the course to it is 230 - 180 = 050. Flying 230 takes you farther away. Turn first to the rough course and refine it once on course [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]].

questions.q: Using Figure 11-28 at 10,000 ft on an ISA +20 day at 65 percent power, you have a 20-knot tailwind. About how much fuel does a 104 NM leg take?
options: About 6.4 gallons
About 7.1 gallons
About 8.1 gallons
About 11.4 gallons
questions.why: At 10,000 ft and ISA +20 the table gives 11.4 GPH and 166 knots TAS [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]]. With the tailwind, GS = 166 + 20 = 186 knots. Time = 104 / 186 = 0.559 hr, and fuel = 0.559 x 11.4 = 6.4 gallons, because fuel goes by time and time by groundspeed [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. 7.1 uses TAS (104 / 166 x 11.4). 8.1 subtracts the tailwind (GS 146).
